nameStory: The Atlantic moonfish gets its dreamy name from its distinctive silvery, disk-shaped body that resembles a glowing full moon when it catches the light underwater. Its scientific name 'setapinnis' means 'bristle fin,' referring to the thread-like extensions on its dorsal and anal fins that trail behind like delicate streamers.
description: The Atlantic moonfish is a stunning, pancake-flat fish with a nearly circular, mirror-bright silver body that looks like it was hammered thin by ocean currents. These compressed beauties typically grow to about 12 inches long and are members of the jack family, known for their speed and agility. With their large eyes and distinctive trailing fin filaments, they're unmistakable when you spot one gliding through coastal waters. Though more common in warmer southern waters, they occasionally venture north to New England during summer months.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely compressed and nearly circular profile, like a silver dinner plate standing on edge - you can barely see the fish from head-on

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, thread-like filaments extend from the front of the dorsal and anal fins, streaming behind like delicate ribbons as the fish swims

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant mirror-silver all over with a metallic sheen that reflects light like polished chrome, with no distinct markings or stripes

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, slightly upturned mouth positioned at the front tip of the head, designed for picking small prey from the water column

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Usually 8-12 inches long when fully grown, with the body height nearly matching the length, creating that distinctive moon-like circular silhouette

habitat: In New England waters, Atlantic moonfish are occasional summer visitors found in shallow coastal areas, harbors, and estuaries with sandy or muddy bottoms. They prefer warm, clear water and are often spotted near piers, jetties, or in protected bays where they hunt for small fish and crustaceans. Look for them in water depths of 10-30 feet, sometimes forming small schools that shimmer like underwater mirrors.

seasonality.spring: Rare in New England waters during spring as water temperatures are still too cool for these warm-water visitors.
seasonality.summer: Peak time to spot moonfish in New England, especially during warm water years when Gulf Stream currents bring them north. Most active during daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: May linger into early fall if water temperatures remain warm, but typically begin moving south as coastal waters cool.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having migrated south to warmer Atlantic and Gulf waters for the winter months.

funFact: Atlantic moonfish can actually change the length of their trailing fin filaments - when threatened or swimming fast, they can retract these delicate streamers into grooves in their fins to avoid damage, then extend them again when cruising leisurely through the water.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small pompano or young permit, but the moonfish's extremely circular body shape and long trailing fin filaments are unique - remember 'moon-shaped with ribbons trailing behind.'
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse the Atlantic moonfish with the Pacific moonfish or other 'moonfish' species from different families - the Atlantic moonfish is specifically a member of the jack family and has a much more compressed, circular body than most other fish called 'moonfish.'
compareHints: The Atlantic moonfish is much more circular and compressed than its close relative the lookdown, which has a more diamond-shaped profile and a distinctly sloped forehead. While both have silvery bodies and trailing fin filaments, the lookdown's body is taller than it is long, whereas the moonfish is nearly perfectly round. The lookdown also has faint vertical bars on its sides that the moonfish lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Atlantic moonfish, the lookdown has a much steeper, more dramatically angled forehead and a smaller, more downward-pointing mouth.
